analysis.one_liner: Bases Social Security raises on a seniors-specific inflation index and extends payroll taxes to wages above the cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in August 2024 with three Democratic cosponsors, referred to three House committees and then a subcommittee, it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would base Social Security's annual cost-of-living increases on a new Consumer Price Index for people 62 and older, which tracks the healthcare and housing costs seniors actually face and typically rises faster than the index used today. It would also apply Social Security payroll taxes to earnings above the annual taxable maximum (about $168,600 in 2024), starting in 2025 under a multiyear schedule set out in the bill text, while giving high earners a small benefit credit for the extra taxes they pay. The aim is bigger annual raises for beneficiaries and more money flowing into a program with long-term financing gaps.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries would get cost-of-living adjustments measured by an index built for seniors' spending, and increases would not count against SSI or Medicaid eligibility. The program's finances would get new revenue from taxes on high earners' wages above the cap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers (CPI-E) tracking the spending of people 62 and older, and makes that index the basis for Social Security cost-of-living increases.
Any benefit increase from the new index would not be counted as income or resources when determining eligibility or benefit amounts for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or Medicaid.

The bill would count a share of wages and self-employment income above the annual contribution and benefit base for Social Security payroll tax purposes, beginning in 2025, with the share for each year set by a table in the bill text.

High earners who pay tax on above-cap earnings would receive a small addition to their benefit formula — 3 percent, then 0.25 percent, of their surplus earnings — under the bill's amended benefit calculation.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people with earnings above the annual Social Security taxable maximum (about $168,600 in 2024) would pay the new tax on income above that cap, and their employers would pay a matching share.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: The bill is a tax increase for high earners: it would subject wages and self-employment income above the annual taxable maximum to Social Security payroll tax starting in 2025, and employers of those workers would owe a matching share.

As printed, the bill text's schedule counts 86 percent of above-cap wages in 2025 and declines each year to zero for years after 2030 — the opposite of a phase-in — so if taken literally the new revenue would disappear after 2030, undercutting the bill's own financing.

Using the seniors-focused CPI-E would raise annual cost-of-living adjustments faster than the current index, increasing program costs over time; the bill counts on the new above-cap tax revenue to cover that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries, the bill offers a more accurate inflation measure — the current index underweights the healthcare spending that dominates senior budgets — plus new revenue for a program whose trust fund faces long-term shortfalls. The cost falls on a narrow group: people earning above roughly $168,600 and their employers. The main design weakness is the bill's own tax schedule, which as written phases down to zero, making the financing hard to take at face value; and the small benefit credit for high earners partially offsets the new revenue. The core trade-off — modestly higher taxes on high earners for stronger, more accurate benefits — is straightforward, but the drafting problems mean it would need reworking before it could work as intended.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from the day it was introduced — referred to three House committees in August 2024 and to the Social Security subcommittee in December — and expired with no hearing, markup, or vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jill Tokuda introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, joined by Reps. Steve Cohen and Jan Schakowsky.
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and additionally to the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce Committees.
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security — the last action recorded before the Congress ended.
The bill had three cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the wage cap and their employers kept the status quo, avoiding the new payroll tax; beneficiaries got neither the seniors-based inflation adjustment nor the new revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the wage cap

for.name: Jill Tokuda
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on the day it was introduced; no markup or hearing was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but with no votes ever held there is no record of how the chambers would have split.

industries.industry: Households earning above the Social Security wage cap (~$168,600 in 2024)
industries.note: The bill would apply Social Security payroll tax to their earnings above the annual cap starting in 2025, under the schedule printed in the bill text. Their added payments are the revenue intended to fund richer COLAs and shore up the program.
Employers pay a matching share of Social Security payroll tax, so taxing above-cap wages would raise their payroll costs as well. The cost falls on businesses with well-paid workforces.
